The maximum fork length attained by bony flyingfish has been documented at 18.0 centimeters [Li = 18.0 centimeters], a value recorded from field surveys across the western Pacific. These measurements indicate that Hirundichthys oxycephalus is a relatively small-bodied exocoetid compared to some congeners. In contrast, the congeneric species Hirundichthys affinis reaches a larger ultimate size, highlighting a marked interspecific difference in growth capacity. The fork length at which 50 percent of individuals have reached puberty is estimated at 12.54 centimeters [Lp = 12.54 centimeters], a value derived from size-at-maturity relationships. This length corresponds to roughly 70 percent of the ultimate fork length, suggesting that sexual maturation occurs at a similar relative size as in related flyingfishes. These size benchmarks are essential for understanding the species' demographic structure and reproductive scheduling.

Neonates of Hirundichthys oxycephalus emerge from fertilised eggs that are remarkably small, with an estimated wet weight at birth of 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams]. This minute mass, comparable to that of a small planktonic invertebrate, reflects the pelagic egg dimensions typical of the genus. The incubation period leading to eclosion is brief under the prevailing thermal regime of the tropical surface waters these fish inhabit. At a water temperature of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C], the age at birth is approximately 2 days [ab = approximately 2 days], a rapid developmental interval that is consistent with the high metabolic rates characteristic of small-bodied, warm-water teleosts. The yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous reserves during this initial phase.

Under the same thermal conditions of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C], females produce clutches of approximately 30 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 30 eggs per spawning event] and exhibit a spawning frequency of roughly 1 spawning event per day [F_R_i = roughly 1 spawning event per day], resulting in a high daily reproductive output. This iteroparous strategy, delivering a continuous stream of small, buoyant eggs into the plankton, is an adaptation to the high early-life mortality typical of pelagic spawners.

The time required for a newly hatched larva to reach the onset of sexual maturity is estimated from growth trajectories recorded in the field. At a stable temperature of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C], the time since birth at puberty is approximately 141 days [tp = approximately 141 days]. This relatively short maturation period allows multiple generations within a single year, a life-history pattern that is common among small, fast-growing epipelagic fishes. The fast pace of development contrasts with longer maturation schedules observed in larger-bodied members of the family Exocoetidae. The period from hatching to reproductive maturity is a critical window during which individuals must acquire sufficient body size and condition.

Based on field surveys and mark-recapture studies, the maximum recorded lifespan for Hirundichthys oxycephalus reaches approximately 548 days [am = approximately 548 days] under the surface-water thermal regime of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C]. This longevity, spanning about one and a half years, is consistent with the rapid life-history syndrome observed in small, short-lived pelagic teleosts. The species appears to experience high natural mortality, driven by predation from larger piscivores such as tunas and billfishes. The combination of a short lifespan, early maturation, and continuous spawning defines a life-history strategy finely tuned to the variable and predation-rich environment of the tropical epipelagic zone.
